title: How to cook okra
seoTitle: Crispy Cornmeal Fried Okra and How to Make Okra Less Slimy
description: A simple cornmeal fried okra recipe, plus easy ways to cut down on okra slime. How we cook the okra from our garden.
summary: Slice fresh okra, dip it in buttermilk, coat it in seasoned cornmeal and shallow fry it at 350°F until golden. To keep okra from getting slimy, cook small, dry pods whole or in a cornmeal coating, cook them hot and fast, or add an acid like tomatoes or vinegar.
targetQueries: how to make okra not slimy
intro: Fried okra is one of our favorite ways to eat the harvest. A crisp cornmeal crust turns young pods into something even okra skeptics go back for.
The best okra for cooking is young and tender, picked at 2 to 5 inches long. For picking and storing pods, see [how to harvest okra](/okra/how-to-harvest-okra).

items: Use young pods, 2 to 5 inches long
Rinse just before cooking, then dry well
Fry in a cornmeal coating at 350°F
Cook hot and fast, or add an acid, to cut the slime

blocks.text: This is a Southern-style fried okra with a buttermilk dip and a cornmeal coating. A little flour helps the cornmeal stick, and a shallow fry in a heavy skillet keeps it simple. It serves 4 as a side.

items: 1 pound fresh okra, about 4 cups sliced
1 cup buttermilk
1 cup fine or medium yellow cornmeal
1/3 cup all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon salt, plus more for finishing
1/2 teaspoon black pepper
1/2 teaspoon garlic powder
1/4 teaspoon cayenne pepper, optional
Vegetable or peanut oil for frying
Rinse the okra and pat it completely dry. Trim off the stems and slice the pods crosswise into 1/2 inch rounds.
Pour the buttermilk into a bowl and add the okra. Stir to coat and let it sit while you mix the coating.
In a second bowl, mix the cornmeal, flour, salt, pepper, garlic powder and cayenne.
Pour about 1/2 inch of oil into a cast iron or other heavy skillet and heat it to 350°F.
Lift a handful of okra out of the buttermilk, let the extra drip off, and toss it in the cornmeal mix until every piece is coated.
Fry in a single layer without crowding the pan, turning once, until golden brown and crisp, about 3 to 4 minutes.
Drain on a wire rack or paper towels and sprinkle with a little salt while hot. Repeat with the rest of the okra, letting the oil come back to 350°F between batches.

blocks.title: Keep it crisp
blocks.text: Fry in small batches. Too much okra at once drops the oil temperature, and the coating soaks up oil instead of crisping. Serve it right away.
Hot oil needs care. Keep a lid nearby, never leave the pan unattended, and never put water on a grease fire. Let the oil cool completely before you strain or throw it out.

If you froze sliced okra coated in cornmeal, it can go straight from the freezer into the hot oil without thawing. It may need an extra minute. See [how to preserve okra](/okra/preserving-okra) for freezing it that way.

sections.title: How to make okra less slimy

blocks.text: Okra's slime comes from mucilage, the natural sugars and soluble fiber in the pods. Clemson Extension notes that it [thickens soups, stews and gumbos](https://hgic.clemson.edu/okra-pickles-and-cornbread/), but not everyone likes it. The way you prepare and cook okra makes a big difference.

items: Pick young pods. Older, larger pods are tougher and stringier.
Rinse right before cooking and dry the pods well. Wet okra steams instead of searing.
Cook small pods whole. The less you cut, the less mucilage gets out.
Cook hot and fast. Frying, roasting, grilling or a quick stir-fry keeps the pods crisp.
Use a cornmeal coating or batter, as in fried okra, hushpuppies, fritters or skillet cornbread.
Add an acid. Clemson lists pickling as one way to tame the slime, and tomatoes or a splash of vinegar help in a stew.

blocks.text: Fried okra isn't the only way we eat it. Young pods are good fresh from the garden after a rinse. We also stir-fry okra with other summer vegetables and pickle a lot of it. For a tested pickled okra recipe, see [how to preserve okra](/okra/preserving-okra).

faq.question: Why is okra slimy?
faq.answer: Okra pods contain mucilage, a mix of natural sugars and soluble fiber that turns gooey when the pods are cut and cooked in liquid. It's what makes okra a good thickener for gumbo.

faq.question: How do you keep fried okra from getting slimy?
faq.answer: Dry the okra well before coating it, fry it in oil that is fully heated to about 350°F, and cook it in small batches so the oil stays hot. A crisp cornmeal crust keeps the slime in check.

faq.question: Can you fry frozen okra?
faq.answer: Yes. Okra that was blanched, sliced, coated in cornmeal and frozen can go straight into the hot oil without thawing. It may take a minute longer to brown.

faq.question: Can you eat okra raw?
faq.answer: Yes. Young, tender pods are good raw. Rinse them under running water first.
